hints: Focus on writing out the full chemical equation that each enthalpy name describes, starting from the correct reactants in their standard states.

Write the equation for burning graphite in oxygen, $\text{C(graphite)} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g})$, then ask what the formation equation for $\text{CO}_2(\text{g})$ looks like.
Check whether the two equations use exactly the same reactants and make exactly the same one mole of product, because then their enthalpy values must match in size.
walkthrough:
**Recall what the names mean**

The key trick is simple. Every standard enthalpy has its own strict recipe for reactants and products.

Formation: 1 mole of compound from elements in standard states. Combustion: 1 mole of substance burned fully in $\text{O}_2$.

**Write the equations for option C**

Combustion of graphite:
$$\text{C(graphite)} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g})$$
Formation of $\text{CO}_2(\text{g})$:
$$\text{C(graphite)} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g})$$
They are the identical reaction, so $\Delta H_c^\ominus = \Delta H_f^\ominus$ for this special case.

**Check why the others do not match**

For the other pairs the equations start or end in different places. Different gaseous atoms versus elements, or $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$ versus $\text{H}_2(\text{g})$, means different energy changes. Only the graphite and $\text{CO}_2$ pair lines up perfectly.

options.A: Incorrect. Atomisation of $\text{CH}_4(\text{g})$ is $\text{CH}_4(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{C(g)} + 4\text{H(g)}$, breaking to gaseous atoms. Formation is $\text{C(graphite)} + 2\text{H}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CH}_4(\text{g})$, starting from elements in standard states. Different reactants and products, so values differ greatly.
options.B: Incorrect. Combustion of $\text{CH}_3\text{OH(l)}$ is $\text{CH}_3\text{OH(l)} + 1.5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The sum $\text{C} + 2\text{H}_2$ combusted gives $\text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ from elements, not from methanol. By Hess cycle the difference between them is the formation enthalpy of methanol, so they are not equal.
options.C: Correct. Both processes are described by the same equation: $\text{C(graphite)} + \text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(\text{g})$. This is complete combustion of one mole of carbon, and it is also formation of one mole of $\text{CO}_2$ from its elements in standard states. Same reaction, so numerically equal.
options.D: Incorrect. Neutralisation is essentially $\text{H}^+(\text{aq}) + \text{OH}^-(\text{aq}) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$, about -57 kJ per mol. Formation of water is $\text{H}_2(\text{g}) + 0.5\text{O}_2(\text{g}) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$, about -286 kJ per mol. Both make water but from completely different starting materials.
